## Built

**[sampler.js](spatialecon-js/src/view/sampler.js) + [f4.js](spatialecon-js/src/scenarios/f4.js)** — the Bundle cycle drawn. Every candidate location one Person sampled, sized and shaded by what it was worth; the one taken ringed; lines to the Firms the basket sources from, weighted by spend. It needed a `watch` hook on `personBundle`, because Bundles are local to a decision everywhere else and shouldn't be retained on 500 People to serve one view.

**[buylines.js](spatialecon-js/src/view/buylines.js)** — the trades themselves rather than their consequences, as a plane overlay. Reads `lastSellers`/`lastQuantities`, so under demand noise it shows what was *bought*, not what was wanted.

**[equalise.js](spatialecon-js/src/view/equalise.js)** — C1's cutoff ring, with the fringe People individually ringed and counted.

**[optimiser.js](spatialecon-js/src/view/optimiser.js)** — A4's second panel: the hill-climber in quantity space, walking the budget line from a random start to the constrained optimum. 165 accepted steps out of 2,000, nearly all early. Needed `lastPath` on `hillClimb`.

## Three findings worth flagging

**The C1 fringe reproduces a third time, and the estimator is the whole game.** Drawing the cutoff forced a choice about how to estimate U\* from a run. Taking the maximum utility is the obvious move and is wrong — it picks the luckiest draw. The **median** is right, because the distribution is a spike at U\* plus a left tail, so the median is U\* for any fringe under half. The check:

| People | Java | JS, median | JS, max |
|---|---|---|---|
| 125 | 43.2% | 44.0% | 93.6% |
| 250 | 20.4% | 20.0% | 48.0% |
| 500 | 7.2% | 7.6% | 18.6% |
| 1000 | 1.9% | 2.0% | 4.9% |

The median column tracks the Java to within a point at every population, from code sharing no line with it. Written into CODE_ANATOMY §5.3.

**F4 gives away something I hadn't expected to be so stark.** The affordable Bundles split into a group of ten all within a few per cent of each other and a handful much worse. So the decision is nearly always between near-equivalents decided by a small margin — which is a good thing to have seen *before* reading chapter 5, since it's why the spatial equilibrium is loose and why a little demand noise is enough to make a Firm misread it. It's in the model's notes.

**F4 needed tuning to teach.** At density radius 1/8 the circles blanket the space, everyone pays everywhere, and the settlement flees to the boundary — true, and C8's mechanism, but it drags the subject off the frame. At 1/12 with cost 60, about a fifth of sampled Bundles come back unaffordable while the population stays interior. The reasoning is in the config comment so it doesn't read as an arbitrary number.

## Built

**Five precomputed sweeps** (`tools/sweep.mjs` → `data/sweeps/*.json`, committed). Rendered by `paintCurves`, which I split out of [curve.js](spatialecon-js/src/view/curve.js) so a swept figure and the live model above it are the same chart rather than two that resemble each other. Two of them are clickable — click a density cost on C8's curve and the settled model above reorganises towards it.

**Pop-outs** in [content.js](spatialecon-js/src/content.js), three kinds per model: *the economics*, *under the hood*, *what we found*. Twenty entries, variants inheriting their family. A test asserts the three models with real disagreements still report them.

**Walkthroughs** on C1, D1, E3, E8 and F4 — captions firing on model state, shown under the canvas.

**The catalogue**: seven groups with a sentence each, and a still per model rendered by the same view code (`npm run thumbs`). **Capture** now composes both panels into one image, as the original's `a` key did.

## Three things worth flagging

**The E3 sweep is a better result than the ramped run.** Holding ρ still instead of ramping it, the efficiency ratio is 1.000 to three decimals up to 0.73, first departs at 0.74, and has clearly gone by 0.75 — where the thesis puts it. The ramped runs break at 0.766 (here) and 0.764 (Java). Both ramps lag, which is what a ramp through a threshold does. So the ramp tells you the model shifts and the sweep tells you where.

**The D1 sweep contradicted the note I'd written for it.** I'd assumed the wandering grows where the incentive is strongest. It's the reverse: at ρ=0.99 the wander is 0.155 at a distance cost of 1 and falls to 0.07 by 20. When goods are near-substitutes and distance is cheap, position barely affects revenue, the crawl has almost no signal, and the Firms roam. The weak-incentive corner is the unreliable one. Corrected before it shipped. It also needed averaging over the back half of each run and over seeds — reading a separation off the final day of a process the thesis says never settles is one draw of a random walk.

**A test caught me breaking my own rule.** Seven walkthrough predicates read `world.day`. Four were openers (now `() => true`), two were C1 startup guards (now a state test — utility is zero until a Person acts, which says "the run has started" without a day number), and three are genuinely *about* elapsed time — "two thousand days in and the Firms are still moving" survives any reseed, because they never settle under any of them. Those declare `elapsed: true`, and the test now fails on any undeclared `world.day` read. That turns BUILD_PLANNER §3.2 from a convention into something enforced.

## One fix that mattered

`.gitignore` had a blanket `data/`, which would have silently excluded the sweeps the site fetches. Now `data/*` with `!data/sweeps/`, and the reason is in the file.

Stage 8 is what's left: C3, C5, C7, E2, E4, C4, F1–F3, G1, and the methodology write-up.

## What's in it

One section per stage, and an entry only earns its place by recording a **decision**, a **finding**, or an **error**. Not a changelog of files touched — that's what the code is for.

The parts that existed nowhere before:

- **The mistakes, with their causes.** The performance estimate that was wrong by an order of magnitude and needed a spatial index. The stale grid that two tests now cover from both directions. The `--shade` default that made a working fix look broken. The D1 sweep whose first version measured one draw of a process that never settles. The seven walkthrough predicates that broke the project's own §3.2 rule and turned it from a convention into an enforced one.

- **A "Corrections to the record" table** — seven places where building something changed a claim in an existing document, with where each now lives. That's the fastest way to check whether an earlier statement has moved, which is otherwise a re-derivation every time.

- **The judgement calls with their reasoning.** Log axes on A1/A4 but not A3. The arrow scatter over a plain scatter. F4's density radius. Median rather than maximum for U\*. Each of those is a decision someone could reasonably second-guess, and the log says why rather than leaving the code to be reverse-engineered.

## Two notes on how I wrote it

I dated by phase — July 2026 for the Java work and planning, 31 July for stages 1–5, 2 August for 5b–7. File mtimes aren't reliable stage markers, since earlier files get edited by later stages (`behaviour.js` gained the F4 watch hook in stage 6), so I used the phases I'm confident about rather than inventing precision.

And I added a line to CLAUDE.md telling future sessions to **append to it as stages land**, with the same "decision, finding or error" test. A build log that's written retrospectively once is a document; one that's appended to is a habit. This one was written retrospectively, which is worth knowing when reading it — the stage 1–4 entries are reconstructed from the code and the conversation, while 5b–7 were written as they happened.

Ready for stage 8 when you are.

 * Load the manifest and every sweep belonging to a model.""",
"""/**
 * A cloud of points rather than a curve.
 *
 * The tomahawk needs this and a line chart cannot carry it: at one transport cost there may
 * be one equilibrium or three, so there is no function to draw, and connecting the points in
 * x order would invent branches that do not exist. Stability is the second encoding — filled
 * black for stable, hollow grey for unstable — which is what turns a scatter into the figure
 * everyone recognises.
 *
 * @param {HTMLCanvasElement} canvas @param {SweepDoc} sweep
 */
function paintScatter(canvas, sweep) {
  const points = sweep.scatter ?? [];
  const { ctx, w, h, dpr } = fitCanvas(canvas);
  if (points.length === 0) return;

  const fontSize = Math.max(Math.round(h * 0.036), 9 * dpr);
  const box = { left: w * 0.12, right: w * 0.97, top: h * 0.07, bottom: h - fontSize * 3.4, dpr };
  const xs = points.map((p) => p.x);
  const ys = points.map((p) => p.y);
  const xRange = padded(Math.min(...xs), Math.max(...xs), 0.02);
  const yRange = padded(Math.min(...ys, 0), Math.max(...ys, 1), 0.04);

  /** @param {number} v */
  const sx = (v) => box.left + ((v - xRange[0]) / (xRange[1] - xRange[0])) * (box.right - box.left);
  /** @param {number} v */
  const sy = (v) => box.bottom - ((v - yRange[0]) / (yRange[1] - yRange[0])) * (box.bottom - box.top);

  drawAxes(ctx, box, xRange, yRange, sx, sy, sweep.xLabel, sweep.yLabel);

  const r = Math.max(1.6 * dpr, 1.4);
  for (const p of points) {
    ctx.fillStyle = p.stable ? '#000' : 'rgba(0,0,0,0.32)';
    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.arc(sx(p.x), sy(p.y), r, 0, Math.PI * 2);
    ctx.fill();
  }

  ctx.font = `${fontSize}px ui-monospace, Menlo, monospace`;
  ctx.textBaseline = 'top';
  ctx.textAlign = 'right';
  ctx.fillStyle = '#000';
  ctx.fillText('stable', box.right, box.top);
  ctx.fillStyle = 'rgba(0,0,0,0.45)';
  ctx.fillText('unstable', box.right, box.top + fontSize * 1.3);
  ctx.textAlign = 'left';
}

/**
 * Load the manifest and every sweep belonging to a model.""")

denominator of U = (w − D(d)) / (p + cd) — and change how much the distance term is worth
relative to the crowding term. Raise the wage and crowding is cheap in proportion, so People
accept more of it and pack in. Raise the base price and the cd term matters proportionally
less, so distance stops being worth paying to avoid. A spatial cost is multiplied by distance

need to model a labour market and a goods market as separate things. That collapse is exactly

C3's config is lost; this is reconstructed from the thesis text on C1's population and space.`,
    async compute() {
      const steps = 9;
      const xs = Array.from({ length: steps }, (_, i) => i / (steps - 1));
      /** @type {Record<string, number[]>} */
      const out = { wage: [], goodCost: [], commute: [], delivery: [] };
      /** @type {[string, string, number, number][]} */
      const sweeps = [
        ['c3w', 'wage', 0.05, 1.5],
        ['c3g', 'goodCost', 0.05, 2.0],
        ['c3c', 'commute', 0, 1.0],
        ['c3d', 'delivery', 0, 1.0],
      ];
      for (const [id, key, from, to] of sweeps) {
        for (const x of xs) {
          const value = from + x * (to - from);
          const scenario = get(id);
          const config = scenario.config();
          if (key === 'wage') config.wage = value;
          else if (key === 'goodCost') config.baseGoodCost = value;
          else if (key === 'commute') config.commuteCost = value;
          else config.deliveryCost = value;
          const world = new World(config);
          scenario.setUp?.(world);
          // No beforeDay: the cost is HELD, so each point is a settled model rather than a
          // moment in a ramp.
          for (let d = 0; d < 1200; d++) world.timeline.nextDay();
          const firm = world.firm(0);
          out[key].push(
            world.people.reduce((a, p) => a + world.distance(p, firm), 0) / world.people.length);
        }
      }
      return {
        xLabel: 'each cost across its own range, normalised',
        yLabel: 'mean distance from the centre',
        xs,
        series: [
          { label: 'wage', values: out.wage },
          { label: 'base good cost', values: out.goodCost, dash: true },
          { label: 'commute', values: out.commute },
          { label: 'goods distance', values: out.delivery, dash: true },
        ],
      };
    },
  },

  {
    id: 'e8-rho',""")
p.write_text(t)

---

## Stage 8 — the rest of the catalogue *(2 August 2026)*

C3, C4, C5, C7, E2, E4, F1, F2, F3, G1, and the methodology write-up. Forty-two models,
which is all of them.

**Over half of these are not agent models**, and that is the catalogue rather than a
shortfall. C4 and C5 are closed forms you could do on paper; E4 is a difference equation with
the agents deliberately removed; F1 and F2 are process demonstrations; G1 is Krugman's Core
Model, a separate program in the original. They are all `Scenario`s anyway, so every model in
the thesis is a page with the same controls, notes and chart machinery — and the ones that
run no agents say so in their first line.

**C3's four signs reproduce.** The published claim is a set of *directions*, and holding each
cost still rather than ramping it gives four clean monotone curves:

| cost | kind | mean distance from centre | direction |
|---|---|---|---|
| wage 0.05 → 1.5 | non-spatial | 0.419 → 0.236 | agglomerating |
| base good cost 0.05 → 2 | non-spatial | 0.121 → 0.331 | **dispersive** |
| commute 0 → 1 | spatial | 0.269 → 0.155 | agglomerating |
| goods distance 0 → 1 | spatial | 0.733 → 0.179 | agglomerating |

The good-cost reversal is the one that is easy to get backwards. Goods getting dearer does not
push People outward by making them poorer; it does it by making the part of the price that
varies with distance a smaller share of the total.

**C7's core swap reproduces, and it is counter-intuitive in the right direction.** Two Firms
1 apart, identical but for distance costs of 2 and 4, with ρ swept down and back. Measured as
mean distance to the cheap Firm minus mean distance to the dear one: −0.37 at ρ = 0.99,
crossing near 0.52, +0.49 at ρ = 0.05. Strong love of variety puts People next to the good
that is *expensive to ship*, importing the cheap one. Modest hysteresis on the return leg.

**E2 needed its markup range corrected, and then said something sharper.** The first build
used a markup three orders of magnitude too small — over-thinking the per-transaction ratchet
— and produced a model where nothing happened. At the thesis' 0–0.15 both endings appear, and
which one you get depends on *how the markup arrives*: ramped slowly it is the squeeze
(Firm 0 to 1.27, Firm 1 down to 0.76, utility 2.5 → 2.1); dropped straight onto 0.15 it is
the runaway (Firm 0 to five thousand, selling nothing, Firm 1 the sole producer at the
one-Firm clearing price).

That also exposed a control bug worth naming, because it is a pattern: a scenario that both
*drives* a parameter and *exposes* it will overwrite the slider on the next day, so the
control appears to work and does nothing. E2 now sets a flag when the slider is touched, which
stops the sweep — and reaching the second ending depends on it.

**The EoS coupling reproduces, and settling time nearly hid it.** The thesis says a markup
changes relative prices only without economies of scale, and absolute prices with them.
Measured at 2,000 days the drag on Firm 1 at zero curve reads 0.002 — not nothing. At 6,000
days it reads 0.0000003. At zero curve the equilibrium price is 1.0 and these runs start near
0.66, so the first measurement was of a run still travelling. The real numbers are 0 / 0.0026
/ 0.0047 at curves 0 / 0.5 / 1.

**E4 is the best model in the tail.** Four pairs of numbers and one line of arithmetic, no
agents at all, both Firms updated simultaneously so the instability cannot be blamed on turn
order. At ρ = 0.73 the perturbation decays to 5.5e-7 and both prices return to 2/3; at 0.80 it
grows to 0.38 and *settles*, at prices 0.527 and 0.907 with production 1.703 against 0.113.
Threshold between 0.73 and 0.76, as the thesis reports. Convergence takes a few thousand steps
against the thesis' sixty, because the constant the law of motion is applied by is a free
choice and this one is smaller — it changes the speed and not the threshold.

**F1 saturates higher than the thesis' run length shows.** At the specified 200,000 exchanges
the Gini is 0.33 and still climbing; five times longer and it reaches 0.48, the exponential
limit this process converges to. Both are "not far off real countries", which is the thesis'
point and its warning.

**F2 gives the teaching number for free.** Only 19 per cent of gaps land within a tenth of a
day of the mean. If the distribution were the spike everyone assumes when writing a t versus
t−1 comparison, it would be 100.

**F3's obvious guess is wrong, and the test now says so.** "Drop α to 1 and the rational
population starts producing" — no. At α = 1 a lone worker produces exactly zero, which is no
better than not working, so correct reasoners stay deadlocked. It breaks at α = 0. The hole is
the threshold *itself*, not its size: any positive α stops a population of correct reasoners
from ever starting. The first version of both the note and the test asserted the wrong thing.

**G1 reproduces the five equilibria and the tomahawk**, and needed one deliberate departure.
The original detects equilibria by walking the wage-ratio curve looking for sign changes,
which cannot see the corner equilibria at λ = 0 and λ = 1 — they are equilibria by
construction rather than by crossing, since with every worker already in one region there is
nobody left to move. Without them the tomahawk is drawn without the two stable branches that
give it its name, so they are computed and added. The port also keeps one oddity rather than
tidying it: on the first iteration the second region's income and price index are read before
being assigned, and Java's zero-initialised arrays supply zero for both. It converges
regardless — but "tidied" is how a port stops matching.

**The methodology write-up** (`methodology.html`) is the §7.4 prose: why an agent's budget is
a day rather than money, the three decision types and which one breaks, agent number as a
modelling assumption rather than a detail, rational agents doing worse than blind ones,
functional versus descriptive mapping, and "showing something is the start of an explanation".
Each section links to the models that demonstrate it. No interactives and no engine support,
as decision 3 settled.

## Where it stands

Forty-two models — the whole catalogue, all seven groups — every one with a view, pop-outs in

models. Seven precomputed sweeps, two of them clickable. A methodology page carrying the

The plan in BUILD_PLANNER §8 is complete.

## Built

C3 (four cost variants), C4, C5, C7, E2, E4, F1, F2, F3, G1, plus [methodology.html](spatialecon-js/methodology.html) — the §7.4 prose, cross-linked to the models that demonstrate each argument.

Over half the tail turned out not to be agent models. C4 and C5 are closed forms; E4 is a difference equation with the agents deliberately removed; F1 and F2 are process demonstrations; G1 is Krugman's Core Model in [coremodel.js](spatialecon-js/src/coremodel.js). They're all `Scenario`s anyway, so every model is a page with the same machinery — and the ones that run no agents say so in their first line.

## What reproduced

**C3's four signs**, holding each cost still rather than ramping it: wage 0.419→0.236 (agglomerating), base good cost 0.121→0.331 (**dispersive**), commute 0.269→0.155, delivery 0.733→0.179. The good-cost reversal is the easy one to get backwards — dearer goods push People outward by making the distance-varying part of the price a smaller share, not by making them poorer.

**C7's core swap**, and it's counter-intuitive in the right direction: strong love of variety puts People next to the good that's *expensive to ship*. Crossing at ρ≈0.52, modest hysteresis on the return leg.

**E4** is the best model in the tail. At ρ=0.73 the perturbation decays to 5.5e-7; at 0.80 it grows to 0.38 and *settles*, one Firm producing 15× the other. Threshold between 0.73 and 0.76, as the thesis says.

**G1's five equilibria** at T=2.25 and the tomahawk's break (T≈1.9) and sustain (≈2.5) points.

## Four things I got wrong and fixed

**E2's markup was three orders of magnitude too small** — I over-thought the per-transaction ratchet. At the thesis' 0–0.15 both endings appear, and which you get depends on *how the markup arrives*: ramped slowly it's the squeeze, dropped straight on it's the runaway.

**The EoS coupling nearly hid behind settling time.** At 2,000 days the drag at zero curve reads 0.002 — most of what the real effect is worth. At 6,000 it reads 0.0000003. The runs simply hadn't arrived.

**F2's pyramid was being sorted into a ramp.** I passed an already-binned histogram to the view's `sorted` mode, which ranked the counts and destroyed the shape. Needed a `bars` mode that leaves the order alone.

**F3's obvious guess is wrong.** "Drop α to 1 and the rational population starts" — no. At α=1 a lone worker produces exactly zero, no better than not working, so correct reasoners stay deadlocked. It breaks at α=0. The hole is the threshold *itself*, not its size. Both the note and the test asserted the wrong thing first; there's now a test that says so explicitly.

## One deliberate departure

The tomahawk was missing its blades. The original detects equilibria by walking the wage-ratio curve for sign changes, which can't see the corners at λ=0 and λ=1 — they're equilibria by construction, not by crossing. Computed and added, and flagged. I did keep one oddity rather than tidying it: the Java reads region 2's income and price index on the first iteration before assigning them, so zero-initialised arrays supply zero. It converges regardless, but tidying is how a port stops matching.

[BUILD_LOG.md](BUILD_LOG.md) has stage 8 and three new rows in the corrections table. Still open, unchanged: D2's ρ direction, the commute round-trip factor, and the fact that C3/C7's exact configs remain unrecoverable even though their results reproduce.

## Assistant

The workflow is ready at [.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml](.github/workflows/deploy-pages.yml). It uploads `spatialecon-js/` as the Pages artifact on every push that touches that folder, so nothing gets moved. Nothing else in the repo gets published: not the thesis sources, the Java, or the planning docs.

## Setting it up

1. Push the repo to GitHub.
2. Go to **Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Source** and pick **GitHub Actions**. That's the only manual step.
3. The first push runs it, or you can use **Actions → Deploy models to GitHub Pages → Run workflow**. The site will be at `https://<you>.github.io/<repo>/`.

## What I checked

- **Every path the site loads works on Pages.** I traced all 112 paths from the three pages, including the ones built at runtime: the sweep JSON and one still per model. All are relative, all stay inside `spatialecon-js/`, and all match their file's case exactly. That last part matters because macOS ignores case differences in filenames and Pages doesn't, so a mismatch would work on your machine and 404 once deployed.
- **It triggers on both `main` and `master`.** Your git has no default branch set, so a plain `git init` gives you `master`, while GitHub's instructions say `main`. A workflow watching the wrong branch never runs and gives no error, so it watches both.
- **It doesn't rebuild anything.** `data/sweeps/` and `snapshots/thumbs/` have to be regenerated and committed locally before you push, the same as now.

I added a short Deploy section to the JS README and a line in CLAUDE.md saying not to move the site into `docs/`.

## Before your first push

Two folders already have their own git repositories inside them, and git won't upload what's in them:

| Folder | Its own repo | State |
|---|---|---|
| `Thesis_on_github/` | linked to `DanOlner/PhD-thesis` | the code folders aren't in that repo yet |
| `ThesisCorrectionsLatex/` | not linked to GitHub | 90 uncommitted changes, 361 MB |

If you run `git init` in `phd_update` and `git add .`, git warns about "embedded git repositories". Each of those folders then shows up on GitHub as an empty, unclickable folder. **The site deploy isn't affected**, because it uses nothing from them. But the GitHub copy of the project won't include the LaTeX sources or the original Java, even though CLAUDE.md points future sessions at both.

You could leave them out deliberately (the LaTeX is large and maybe not something you want public), add them to a root `.gitignore`, or delete their inner `.git` folders so their files get added normally. That's your call. I haven't touched either folder.

I'd still say the most useful thing before or right after the first deploy is to click through it in a browser. Everything so far has been checked without one.
